prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade shocks reshape labour demand, wage inequality and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: The central claim of this body of work is that technology and trade reshape labour demand and the wage structure, and that the effects can be measured credibly. The skill-biased and task-based accounts changed how economists think about inequality. The import-competition evidence showed that local labour markets adjust slowly and at real cost, which overturned the assumption of frictionless reallocation. The influence runs well beyond labour economics into macro, trade and public policy, including today's automation debate. The work is also mature. The technology strand is decades old and the China-shock strand is more than a decade old. Both have been replicated, criticised and refined, and the core findings have survived. Autor spans both strands, Hanson anchors the trade-shock evidence and Katz anchors the long-run technology and wages evidence. As a growth and structural-change economist, I value work that links long-run technological change to distributional outcomes using disciplined evidence. I apply the same standards to B006 and B036 and do not rely on field affinity.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that the ballot bundles two related but distinct discoveries, skill-biased and task-based technology effects and the trade shock. A three-name cap forces an arbitrary split between them. Dorn is a core co-author of the China-shock papers and is left out. Katz's skill-premium work overlaps with the earlier Goldin recognition, and the task framework overlaps with the 2024 prize to Acemoglu and colleagues. The shift-share identification and the persistence and magnitude of the local effects are still debated. If the Committee decides that attribution cannot be made clean, B006 is the stronger-attributed alternative on a narrower and more theoretically foundational discovery.

responses.point: John Hassler proposes only Kiyotaki and Moore for B006. He argues that Gertler's accelerator work builds on Bernanke-Gertler, that Bernanke's 2022 prize already covers part of that line, and that a two-person award is the cleanest attribution.
responses.response: I agree this is the sharper attribution case, and it corrects my own opening three-name proposal for B006. The collateral-constraint mechanism of Kiyotaki and Moore is cleanly identified. Gertler's credit is partly tied to work that cannot be recognised again. I would support the two-name version if the Committee settled on B006. I still place B023 first. Its attribution problem is of a different kind, since it comes from the three-name cap and not from an earlier laureate absorbing the credit. I also note that the B006 ballot's own maturity and overlap arguments (the 2022 prize) do not favour it on the criteria we share.

responses.point: Per Strömberg ranks B023 third and proposes only Autor and Hanson. He argues that the task framework and the China-shock work are separate strands, that Katz shares credit with Acemoglu, Goldin and Murphy outside the list, and that Autor and Hanson give the tightest attribution.
responses.response: I take the bundling concern seriously, and it is my main reservation. I disagree with dropping Katz. The long-run skill-biased technical change and wage-structure evidence is the empirical foundation on which the task and trade-shock work builds. Without Katz, the citation would cover only the later strands. The cost is the Goldin overlap, but that prize recognised the education and gender strand of his work, and the technology-and-wages contribution is distinct from it. Autor and Hanson alone would fit a narrower citation on trade and labour adjustment. I would then ask whether Dorn should replace Katz rather than leave the pair incomplete, because he co-authored the China-shock papers.

responses.point: Anna Dreber ranks B023 first. She proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn, which treats the China shock as the core discovery. She notes that Autor's task work overlaps with Katz, Goldin and Acemoglu and is therefore entangled with work already honoured.
responses.response: We agree on the ranking, and the Autor-Hanson-Dorn trio has the cleanest single-discovery logic. The trio is the better choice if the Committee wants one tightly defined achievement. I weigh it differently because the case for this ballot rests on how technology and trade jointly change labour demand. Autor spans both strands, and Katz anchors the technology side that the trio would not credit. The overlap you describe is real, and I treat it as a reason to word the citation carefully, not as a reason to drop that strand. I would not object to Dorn instead of Katz if the Committee prefers the narrower citation, and I regard this as an open attribution choice.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee views technology and trade as one coherent achievement or as two that should not share a single citation.
Whether Katz or Dorn is the better third name. I lean to Katz, but the choice is close and I rely on background knowledge and not on verified contribution data.
How much overlap with Goldin (2023) and Acemoglu (2024) should count against the technology and tasks strand.
How far the shift-share identification critiques and the debate over the size and persistence of local effects qualify the China-shock findings.
Whether B006, with an uncontested core mechanism, should take priority over B023 if attribution in B023 cannot be settled.
statement.conflict_note: From my profile: I co-author frequently with Per Krusell and have co-authored with John Hassler, both fellow committee members, and I am a colleague of both at IIES. I have a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow, a credited name in B034, which is not in my preferred configuration. My research uses heterogeneous-agent macro methods related to B043. None of the credited names in B023 appears among my listed co-authors, so no recusal-relevant connection to my preferred configuration is apparent from the supplied profile.
